title: Hope
hookLine: hope is not optimism but confidence in God's promise

cards: The city has fallen. The walls are down, the streets are empty, and the poet who wrote the Book of Lamentations doesn't pretend otherwise. For two long chapters and into a third, he weeps.
He says God has walled him in, made his chains heavy, shut out his prayer. There is nothing in sight to be optimistic about. And then, right in the middle of the book, the voice turns.
Not because anything outside has changed. The rubble is still there. He turns because he remembers something.
That turn is the second of the three virtues.

teach.b: Here's what he remembers, in the King James Bible: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
His hope doesn't come from the news, or from a feeling that things are looking up.
It comes from God's character, and God's promise. That's the difference between optimism and hope as Christians speak of it. Optimism reads the situation and expects it to improve.
Hope can read the same situation, see no improvement at all, and still lean forward, because it rests on who God is.

teach.h: HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.
teach.b: Paul puts it bluntly in Romans: "hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?" If you can already see it, you don't need hope. Hope is for the dark stretch.

Then the letter to the Hebrews gives hope its picture, the one in today's line: "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast." An anchor doesn't stop the storm or calm the water.
It holds the ship in place while the storm goes on, so the ship isn't driven onto the rocks. Hope, in this picture, doesn't make the night shorter. It keeps you from being carried off by it.

how: Christians speak of hope as confidence in God's promises rather than a prediction; Lamentations 3:22–23 is sung in some churches as the hymn 'Great Is Thy Faithfulness', and some Christians use the anchor of Hebrews 6:19 as a symbol of hope.

o: leaning on God's promise even when nothing looks better
a wish for good luck when the odds look bad
a confident forecast that things will soon improve

p: hope that is seen is not hope
reads the news and expects better

s: in Lamentations, hope returns because the city is rebuilt
the rubble is still there. he hopes because he remembers God's mercies.
Paul says hope is for what can't yet be seen
"hope that is seen is not hope."
Hebrews pictures hope as a sail that speeds the ship along
it pictures an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast.

games.q: you're the poet of Lamentations. your city is in ruins, and you've wept through chapter after chapter. nothing outside has changed. what comes next?
o: keep writing grief to the very end.
insist things aren't really so bad.
remember God's mercies, and hope anyway.
games.why: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." the rubble stays, and the turn comes from memory, not from the view.

practice: Find one thing you're waiting for that you can't see yet, someone's healing, a reconciliation, a change in yourself that's slow in coming, and name it quietly in one sentence, without measuring the odds.
Rest your breath on it, the way an anchor rests on the seabed: heavy, still, holding. If you pray, you can borrow the poet's words: this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.
And if the dark feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Hope. In the New Testament's Greek, elpis. Not a forecast that things will improve, but a confident leaning on God's promise in the dark.

orig.note: Greek: hope, the word in Hebrews 6:19 and in Paul's faith, hope and love.

carryVoice: Your line: hope is an anchor. It holds while the storm goes on. Go gently.
